body: 1989 letter, called his 'most surprising discovery': 'rationality frequently wilts when the institutional imperative comes into play.' Four forms, verbatim: '(1) As if governed by Newton's First Law of Motion, an institution will resist any change in its current direction; (2) Just as work expands to fill available time, corporate projects or acquisitions will materialize to soak up available funds; (3) Any business craving of the leader, however foolish, will be quickly supported by detailed rate-of-return and strategic studies prepared by his troops; and (4) The behavior of peer companies, whether they are expanding, acquiring, setting executive compensation or whatever, will be mindlessly imitated.' Cause is 'Institutional dynamics, not venality or stupidity'. The 1990 letter applies it to banks: lenders 'played follow-the-leader with lemming-like zeal; now they are experiencing a lemming-like fate', and at 20x assets/equity 'mistakes that involve only a small portion of assets can destroy a major portion of equity.' Berkshire's response: concentrate in companies 'alert to the problem'. Actionable checklist for Indian companies: cash pile growing + 'diversification' into unrelated areas (imperative #2); every peer announcing the same capex (#4, e.g., capacity waves in cement, steel, specialty chem, NBFC loan books); CEO pet projects with consultant decks (#3). Also: 'We've never succeeded in making a good deal with a bad person.'
title: Buffett 1989: the 'institutional imperative' - four ways rational managers go wrong

body: Question: did v1/v2's live-only universe (today's NSE list) bias Indian PEAD? Universe ALL = v1's 700-firm live sample + a same-rate (39%) sample of the 377 NSE quarterly filers of 2018-25 missing from v1's frame (347 dead/left, 30 off-series): 147 sampled, 41 contributed 468 events (4.6% of 10,242). Same standalone-EPS SUE and dates (NSE still serves dead firms' filings + XBRL); weekly closes for everyone (screener for dead firms; LIVE re-run on weekly closes); delisted firms' returns run to the last traded close. 13 weeks, 2018-2025, 32 quarters: H1 bottom quintile vs size-matched controls ALL -2.43% [-3.18,-1.66] t -6.17 -> SUPPORTED (LIVE weekly -2.08%); holds 2018-21 (-3.07%) and 2022-25 (-1.78%), at 4/26 weeks and under -30% delisting penalty or survivors-style drop. H2 top net of 1% +1.00% [-0.03,+2.20] t 1.72 -> NOT PROVEN (third time). H3 bias ALL-LIVE: bottom -0.35pp [-0.82,+0.06], top +0.25pp, T-B +0.57pp [-0.01,+1.19]; none material by the rule; larger in 2018-21 (bottom -0.66pp). Mechanism: dead firms' events deepen the bottom leg (-0.56pp) while dead firms in the control pool lower control returns (+0.2pp to all excess). Why mild (unlike L28 pledges): most failures were already below Rs 400-500 cr (49 of 80 sampled distress-listed firms never reached the band) and most stop filing before trading stops. Descriptive: distress-listed firms after a bottom-two-quintile result -16.6% vs controls in 13 weeks (71 events, 16 firms) -> pair PEAD avoid flag with solvency/pledge flags. Weekly closes cost ~0.3pp per leg vs daily (v1 same firms -2.42/+2.08). Research, not SEBI-registered advice.
title: Indian PEAD survivorship check (pre-registered): adding dead/delisted firms makes the avoid leg slightly STRONGER (-2.43% vs -2.08% at 13 weeks, t -6.2); long leg still not proven net of 1%; bias mild, not material
